key_terms.meaning: A cyclic device that takes heat Q₁ from a hot reservoir, converts part into work W and rejects Q₂ to a cold reservoir.
A large body whose temperature stays fixed when heat enters or leaves it.
The source supplies heat at high temperature; the sink receives heat at low temperature.
For a heat engine, η = W/Q₁ = (Q₁ − Q₂)/Q₁.
Reversed heat engines that use work W to move heat from a cold region to a hot region.
COP_R = Q₂/W for a refrigerator; COP_HP = Q₁/W for a heat pump.
For the same two reservoirs and the same work input, the heat-pump COP is one more than the refrigerator COP.
A supposed cyclic machine that converts all heat from one reservoir into work; the second law forbids it.
No cyclic device can convert all heat from a single reservoir into work.
No cyclic device can transfer heat from a cold body to a hot body without external work.
A process that can be reversed so both system and surroundings return exactly to their initial states with no net change.
A process whose reverse would leave a permanent change in the system or surroundings.
A reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes between two reservoirs.
No engine between two fixed reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine; all reversible engines have the same efficiency.
A scale defined by T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂ for a reversible engine, independent of the working substance.
For any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, with equality only for a reversible cycle.
A property S defined by dS = δQ_rev/T for a reversible path; it measures disorder and irreversibility.
For any process, ΔS_total = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings ≥ 0, with equality only for a reversible process.
At absolute zero the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero, and absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
A refrigeration capacity unit equal to 3.517 kW of heat removal.

takeaways: The first law balances energy; the second law decides which energy transfers are possible and in which direction they occur.
A cyclic heat engine must reject some heat to a sink, so its thermal efficiency is always less than 100%.
COP can be greater than 1, and for the same reservoirs COP_HP = COP_R + 1.
The Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements are equivalent, and each forbids a different version of a perpetual-motion machine of the second kind.
Reversibility is an ideal limit; friction, finite temperature difference, unrestrained expansion and mixing create irreversibility.
Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_L/T_H is the upper bound for any cycle working between T_H and T_L.
Entropy is defined by dS = δQ_rev/T; for an irreversible path, use a reversible path between the same end states to find ΔS.
The total entropy of system plus surroundings never decreases, and every real process generates entropy.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress the two second-law statements and their equivalence, the Carnot cycle and theorem, the Clausius inequality, entropy change in reversible and irreversible processes, and the principle of increase of entropy.

bank.q: Define a heat engine, a refrigerator and a heat pump. Draw their energy-flow diagrams and show that COP_HP = COP_R + 1 when both work between the same two reservoirs.
outline: Define each device and label Q₁, Q₂ and W.
Draw source, sink and work arrows for engine, refrigerator and heat pump.
Use Q₁ = Q₂ + W for the same reservoirs.
Write COP_R = Q₂/W and COP_HP = Q₁/W.
Substitute to get COP_HP = COP_R + 1.

bank.q: State the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements of the second law. Explain why each statement rules out a different impossible machine.
outline: State Kelvin-Planck statement clearly.
Explain that it forbids a PMM2.
State Clausius statement clearly.
Explain that it forbids heat flow from cold to hot with no work input.
Mention that the two statements are equivalent.

bank.q: Define reversible and irreversible processes. List four causes of irreversibility and give one engineering example of each.
outline: Define reversible process with no trace left in system or surroundings.
Define irreversible process as one whose reverse leaves a permanent change.
List friction, finite temperature difference, unrestrained expansion and mixing.
Give one practical example for each cause.
Explain that all real processes are irreversible.

bank.q: Describe the Carnot cycle with p-V and T-s diagrams. Derive η_Carnot = 1 − T₂/T₁ for an ideal gas.
outline: Name the two isothermal and two adiabatic processes.
Draw p-V and T-s diagrams with heat transfer directions.
Write Q₁ at T₁ and Q₂ at T₂.
Use ideal-gas relations for the four processes.
Derive efficiency as 1 − T₂/T₁.

bank.q: A Carnot engine receives 900 kJ/min from a reservoir at 750 K and rejects heat at 300 K. Find its efficiency, work output per minute and heat rejected per minute.
outline: Use η = 1 − T₂/T₁.
Substitute 300 K and 750 K to get η = 0.6.
Find W = ηQ₁ = 540 kJ/min.
Find Q₂ = Q₁ − W = 360 kJ/min.
State units clearly.

bank.q: A refrigerator keeps a cold room at 2°C while the surroundings are at 35°C. The cooling load is 4 kW and the actual COP is 2.8. Find the compressor work and heat rejected, and compare the actual COP with the Carnot COP.
outline: Convert temperatures to kelvin: 275 K and 308 K.
Use W = Q_L/COP = 1.43 kW.
Use Q_H = Q_L + W = 5.43 kW.
Compare actual 2.8 with ideal 8.33 and mention irreversibility.

bank.q: 0.5 kg of water is heated reversibly at constant pressure from 300 K to 350 K. Take c_p = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K). Find the entropy change of the water.
outline: Use ΔS = m c_p ln(T₂/T₁).
Substitute m = 0.5 kg and c_p = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K).
Use T₂/T₁ = 350/300.
Calculate ΔS = 0.322 kJ/K.
State that entropy increases on heating.

bank.q: One kg of air expands reversibly and isothermally at 400 K from 3 bar to 1 bar. Take R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). Find the entropy change of the air and the heat absorbed.
outline: For isothermal ideal gas, Δs = R ln(P₁/P₂).
Substitute R = 0.287 and pressure ratio 3.
Find Δs = 0.315 kJ/(kg·K).
Use q = TΔs for reversible isothermal process.
Find q = 126 kJ/kg.

bank.q: A cyclic device receives 800 kJ at 500 K, rejects 500 kJ at 300 K and produces 300 kJ of work. Test it with the first law and Clausius inequality; state whether it is reversible, irreversible or impossible.
outline: Check first law: 800 − 500 = 300 kJ, so energy balance is satisfied.
Get −0.067 kJ/K, which is less than zero.
A negative value means the cycle is irreversible.
Conclude that the device is possible but irreversible.

bank.q: Show that two reversible engines operating between the same two reservoirs must have the same efficiency, and hence prove Carnot's theorem.
outline: Assume two reversible engines A and B with different efficiencies.
Couple them so the more efficient engine drives the less efficient one reversed.
Obtain net work while exchanging heat with one reservoir only.
Show this violates the Kelvin-Planck statement.
Conclude that all reversible engines have equal efficiency and no engine beats Carnot.

bank.q: A firm claims an engine with efficiency 45% working between 600 K and 320 K. Evaluate the claim using Carnot's theorem and entropy.
outline: Find Carnot efficiency = 1 − 320/600 = 46.7%.
Compare claimed 45% with 46.7%.
Claimed efficiency is below the Carnot limit, so it is not forbidden by the second law.
It is lower than reversible efficiency, so the engine is irreversible.
Entropy generation is positive.

bank.q: Derive the Clausius inequality from the definition of entropy and explain why ∮δQ/T < 0 for an irreversible cycle.
outline: Write dS = δQ_rev/T for a reversible path.
For a reversible cycle, show ∮δQ/T = 0.
For an irreversible cycle, compare with a reversible path between the same states.
Introduce entropy generation as positive.
Conclude ∮δQ/T < 0 for an irreversible cycle.

bank.q: Discuss the third law of thermodynamics, absolute entropy, and unattainability of absolute zero. Explain why reaching 0 K would need infinite work or steps.
outline: State that a perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K.
Explain absolute entropy by integrating δQ_rev/T from 0 K.
State the unattainability of absolute zero.
Explain that cooling becomes harder as T approaches 0 K.
Conclude that 0 K is a limiting state, not a reachable state.

bank.q: Compare Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements. Explain PMM2 and show how entropy generation measures irreversibility in real devices.
outline: State both second-law statements.
Explain equivalence by contradiction.
Define PMM2 and why it is impossible.
Define entropy generation from ΔS_total.
Use examples such as friction and finite temperature difference to show positive entropy generation.

glossary.def: A body large enough that its temperature remains constant when heat is added or removed.
A thermal reservoir at high temperature that supplies heat to a device.
A thermal reservoir at low temperature that receives rejected heat.
A cyclic device that converts part of the heat taken from a source into work.
The ratio of work output to heat input of a heat engine, η = W/Q₁.
A device that uses work to remove heat from a cold region and reject it to a warmer region.
The ratio of useful heat transfer to work input for a refrigerator or heat pump.
A reversed heat engine used to deliver heat to a warm space.
A refrigeration capacity equal to 3.517 kW of heat removal.
A perpetual-motion machine of the second kind, which would convert all heat from one reservoir into work in a cycle.
No cyclic device can produce work by exchanging heat with only one reservoir.
Heat cannot move from a cold body to a hot body in a cycle without work input.
An ideal process that can be reversed without leaving any net change in system or surroundings.
A real process that leaves a permanent change and cannot be fully reversed.
A process in which irreversibilities occur only outside the system boundary.
The reversible cycle made of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes between two reservoirs.
No engine between two fixed reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine.
A temperature scale based on reversible heat transfers, T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂.
For any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, with equality only for a reversible cycle.
A thermodynamic property whose change for a reversible path is dS = δQ_rev/T.
The extra entropy created by irreversibilities within a process.
A plot of temperature against entropy used to show heat transfer and cycle performance.
The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
The entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at absolute zero.
Entropy measured from the zero set by the third law at 0 K.
Absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of cooling steps.
